content: The South African tuberculosis (TB) program initiates treatment for approximately 10,000 patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) annually. This review examines two distinct datasets: one from patients treated in 2017 using a bedaquiline-based oral regimen, and another from 2019, which included both bedaquiline and linezolid in the oral regimen. Introduction of Bedaquiline-Based Short-Course Regimens In January 2017, South Africa introduced a 9–12 month short-course regimen for MDR/RR-TB, replacing injectable antibiotics with bedaquiline. The regimen consisted of bedaquiline, levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, ethionamide, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, high-dose isoniazid, and clofazimine. Approximately 5% of patients also received linezolid. Patients not meeting these criteria were treated with an 18–24 month bedaquiline-containing regimen. Data Linkage for Relapse and Mortality Follow-up data for all South African cohorts were obtained through the Electronic Drug-Resistant TB Register (EDRWeb) and routine mortality reporting. Patients were tracked using unique identifiers, allowing identification of retreatment cases. Deaths were classified as occurring during or after treatment. The EDRWeb database provided information on demographics, treatment history, HIV status, antiretroviral therapy, drug resistance testing, and treatment outcomes. Transition to Linezolid-Containing Regimens From mid-2018, ethionamide was replaced with linezolid for two months in the regimen due to high resistance rates (7%) and adverse effects like nausea and vomiting. The 2019 cohort included patients treated with a 9–12 month oral regimen containing bedaquiline and linezolid. This regimen was widely adopted by 2019, and follow-up data were largely complete. Eligibility criteria included rifampicin resistance, rifampicin mono-resistance with isoniazid susceptibility, or MDR-TB with specific genetic mutations and susceptibility to fluoroquinolones and injectables. Patients with poor prognostic factors received a longer regimen of 18–24 months. Modified Regimens for Specific Populations For children aged 12 years or older (weighing ≥30 kg), bedaquiline was administered for at least six months, extendable to nine months if smear or culture conversion was delayed. For children aged 6–12 years (weighing 15–30 kg), delamanid replaced injectables. For children under six years (weighing <15 kg), the regimen included para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) instead of bedaquiline or delamanid. Patients with persistent culture positivity on the 9–12 month regimen could transition to the longer regimen. Longer Regimens and Modifications The standard longer regimen (≥18 months) included bedaquiline, levofloxacin, linezolid, terizidone, and clofazimine. Modifications were made for patients with rifampicin-resistant TB meningitis, resistance to key drugs, or low hemoglobin levels (<8 g/dL). Persistent culture positivity on the shorter regimen also warranted transition to the longer regimen. Analytical Considerations The 2019 South African cohort was divided into short-course and longer-course treatment groups based on clinical and microbiological characteristics. Confounding by indication was likely, making direct comparisons of regimen effectiveness within the South African dataset challenging. Comparisons with external cohorts required adjustment for differences in disease severity and follow-up duration. The high prevalence of HIV in the South African cohort necessitated adjustments for HIV status in comparative analyses. WHO Individual Patient Data (IPD) and External Comparisons The WHO IPD dataset from 2021 included 14 datasets of patients treated with standardized oral regimens (18–24 months) containing bedaquiline, with some also including linezolid. These datasets served as external comparators for evaluating shorter regimens. However, differences in follow-up times and patient characteristics introduced potential confounding and selection bias. Clinical Trials and Studies Several clinical trials, including the NEXT trial, NIX-TB study, and ZENIX study, evaluated shorter regimens for MDR/RR-TB. The NEXT trial assessed a 6–9 month regimen in South Africa, while the NIX-TB study focused on a 6-month regimen for extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) or treatment-intolerant MDR-TB. The ZENIX study evaluated varying doses and durations of linezolid in combination with bedaquiline and pretomanid for XDR-TB and pre-XDR-TB. These studies highlighted the potential of shorter regimens but faced challenges such as lack of internal comparator groups and high HIV prevalence among participants. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate outcomes at later time points. Conclusion The review underscores the importance of tailoring TB treatment regimens to patient characteristics and disease severity. Shorter regimens offer the potential for reduced treatment duration and improved adherence but require robust follow-up to monitor relapse and long-term outcomes.
